In the nineteenth century the struck dulcimer was rare in the Appalachian region of America, and the word dulcimer, familiar from the King James Bible, came to mean a three- or four-string fretted instrument usually played on the lap. In the twentieth century many derivatives appeared, including the banjo dulcimer, with a banjo-type resonating membrane; the resonator dulcimer, with a built-in conical resonator; the bowed dulcimer, held upright and played with a bow; and the electric dulcimer, amplified with pickups.

The word dulcimer refers to two families of chordophones: one is the trapezoid zither like the psaltery, with many strings struck by small hand-held hammers, used in folk and classical line-ups and found in cultures including England, Scotland, the United States, southern Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Ukraine, Jewish, Romanian, Hungarian, Greek, Iranian, Iraqi, northern Indian, Pakistani, Cambodian, Lao, Thai, Chinese, Vietnamese and Korean; the other is the three- or four-string fretted instrument of the American Appalachian region, usually played on the lap, from which banjo-type, resonator-type, bowed and electric variants have developed.
德西馬琴名稱涵蓋兩類：一類為手持小槌敲擊的梯形齊特琴，見於英格蘭、蘇格蘭、美國，: The name dulcimer covers two: one is the trapezoid zither struck with small hand-held hammers, found in England, Scotland and the United States, and in southern Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Ukraine, Ashkenazi Jewish, Romanian, Hungarian, Greek, Ottoman, Iranian, Iraqi, northern Indian, Pakistani, Cambodian, Lao, Thai, Chinese, Vietnamese and Korean cultures, as a small folk instrument or a larger classical one. The other is a three- or four-string fretted instrument of the American Appalachian region in the nineteenth century, mostly played on the lap, from which banjo-type, resonator-type, bowed and electric variants developed.

The struck dulcimer is usually set in front of the player and the strings are struck with small hand-held hammers. The Appalachian dulcimer is usually laid on the lap and strummed. The bowed type is held upright and bowed. A beginner should first establish which type the instrument is, then choose the way of holding and sounding that goes with it.
